text: $TSLA investors may be watching revenue while missing the share count. The latest filed year-end count rose 16.6% YoY; $AAPL fell 2.3%. That is not a verdict, but per-share growth should always be read beside issuance, compensation, M&A and buybacks. What explains the gap?
I published the filed histories, fiscal dates, comparability warnings and downloadable dataset here: https://www.stockportfolio.pro/research/shares-outstanding

Share count is one of the easiest financial signals to oversimplify. A rising count can reflect stock compensation, acquisitions, conversions or capital raising. A falling count can reflect net repurchases. Neither direction proves value creation or destruction by itself.

I published a public research layer showing the filed year-end count, exact period, latest-year change, long-run context, repurchase spending and comparability warnings. The dataset is downloadable so the screen can be reproduced.

Apple's 2025 net income was $112.0B. Operating cash flow was $111.5B—almost exactly 1x cash conversion.

The useful bit is the trend: 1.41x in 2020, 1.26x in 2024, 1.00x in 2025.

Not a red flag by itself. Just a reminder to read earnings beside cash. $AAPL

Apple reported $112.01B of FY2025 net income and $111.48B of operating cash flow. Free cash flow after $12.72B of capex was $98.77B.

The useful question is not simply “good or bad?” It is whether the cash kept pace with the accounting earnings. Here it almost exactly did. $AAPL

text:
Apple’s fiscal 2025 net income was $112.01B. Operating cash flow was $111.48B, while free cash flow after $12.72B of capex was $98.77B.

That does not produce a buy or sell answer. It answers a narrower and more useful question: did reported earnings convert into cash over the same filed period? In this case, operating cash flow was almost exactly 1x net income.
